  pagetitle: "Signals and Return Forecasts"
  description-meta: "Building tactical return signals from momentum, the yield curve and cross-sectional turbulence, testing them in and out of sample with the Campbell-Thompson R-squared and the Clark-West statistic, and pricing a tilt on the policy portfolio after costs, in R."

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("R/_common.R")
library(tidypm)
library(knitr)
```

Can the excess return on an asset class be forecast, and does a forecast that
fits the past help an investor who must act on it before the future arrives?
@welch2008 put the first question to every predictor the literature had
proposed for the equity premium and found that hardly any of them would have
helped an investor in real time: the regressions fit in sample and failed out
of sample. @campbell2008 replied that the same predictors do help, by a small
but economically meaningful margin, once the forecast is constrained by what
theory says its sign must be, and between them the two papers fixed the terms
on which every later claim of predictability is judged: an out-of-sample $R^2$
against the historical mean, and the certainty-equivalent gain of an investor
who uses the forecast.

This is the first **tactical** chapter of the book in the sense of
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory: the inputs are conditioned on
information available at the time rather than estimated unconditionally, and
the question is whether the conditioning is worth anything. We first set out
the predictive regression and its two $R^2$ statistics, the test of one
forecast against another, and the economic-value criterion; then say which
signals this universe can carry and build them from the shipped data, momentum
from the return histories and the term spread, the credit spread and a
turbulence index from the bond curve factors and the cross-section; then test
each signal in sample and out of sample, one at a time and combined through an
elastic net; and finally scale the forecasts into a monthly tilt around the
equal-weight policy and price it after costs.

The data are the sixteen risky class series of
@sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market, in excess of the Treasury bill for
the reasons of @sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory, and the assertion
that the bill's dates are the return dates is the first of several in this
chapter that exist because a signal one month out of place produces a
plausible table.

```{r}
#| label: data
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)   # sixteen risky classes
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return                                  # the bill
Re <- R - rf                                                       # excess returns
N  <- ncol(Re); dates <- zoo::index(R)
stopifnot(N == 16L, !anyNA(Re), all(sim_riskfree_monthly$date == dates))
```

## Predictability, In Sample and Out {#sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-theory}

### The predictive regression

Write $r^e_{t+1}$ for the excess return on one series over month $t+1$ and
$\boldsymbol{x}_t$ for a vector of $K$ signals observed by the end of month
$t$. The predictive regression is

$$
r^e_{t+1} = a + \boldsymbol{b}'\boldsymbol{x}_t + \varepsilon_{t+1},
$$ {#eq-16-predictive}

and its in-sample $R^2$ is the share of the variance of $r^e$ that the fitted
values account for over the whole sample,

$$
R^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum_{t}\hat{\varepsilon}_{t+1}^2}
               {\sum_{t}\left(r^e_{t+1} - \bar{r}^e\right)^2},
$$ {#eq-16-r2}

with $\bar{r}^e$ the full-sample mean. Three things about @eq-16-predictive are
settled before any signal is chosen. The dating is the whole of the
discipline: $\boldsymbol{x}_t$ must be known when the position for $t+1$ is
taken, and @sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-implementation asserts that alignment
in code rather than trusting it. The $R^2$ will be small, because
@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-theory showed, following @merton1980, that a mean
is known only to within $\sigma/\sqrt{\tau}$ over $\tau$ years, and a
conditional mean that moves with $\boldsymbol{x}_t$ is a fraction of a number
that is itself barely visible: one percent a month is a strong result in this
literature. And the slope is biased when the signal is persistent and its
innovations are correlated with the return's, as for every valuation ratio
and most yields; @stambaugh1999 derived the bias and @cochrane2008 showed that
the same persistence constrains what the joint system of return and signal can
say. Inference uses the @newey1987 standard errors of @eq-05-neweywest, and
with sixteen series and four signals the sixty-four regressions below are a
multiple-testing problem of the kind @harvey2016 describe, so a $t$-statistic
of two begins a case rather than ending one.

### The out-of-sample $R^2$

An in-sample fit estimates $a$ and $\boldsymbol{b}$ on the whole history and
scores the fitted values on the same history. An investor cannot do that. At
the end of each month $t$ she has the data through $t$, estimates
@eq-16-predictive on them, and forecasts $\hat{r}^e_{t+1}$; the alternative
that uses no signal is the historical mean through $t$, $\bar{r}^e_t$, the
strategic input of @sec-06-expected-returns-theory re-estimated each month.
@campbell2008 score the two sequences of forecasts against each other over
the out-of-sample months $t = T_0, \dots, T-1$ by

$$
R^2_{\text{OS}} = 1 -
  \frac{\sum_{t=T_0}^{T-1}\left(r^e_{t+1} - \hat{r}^e_{t+1}\right)^2}
       {\sum_{t=T_0}^{T-1}\left(r^e_{t+1} - \bar{r}^e_t\right)^2},
$$ {#eq-16-r2os}

which is positive when the signal's forecast errors are smaller than the
mean's and negative when they are larger. Unlike @eq-16-r2 it has no floor at
zero, and a negative value is the common case: @welch2008 report it for most
predictors over most periods, @goyal2024 find on data through 2021 that
almost nothing proposed since fares better, and @mclean2016 show that the
cross-sectional predictors which did work decay after publication. The burn-in
$T_0$ is a choice, and the window can roll or expand; an expanding window uses
everything the investor knows, and it is what we use. @campbell2008 also
restricted the forecast by theory, setting a negative forecast of the equity
premium to zero, and found that the restriction turns most of their negative
$R^2_{\text{OS}}$ positive; exercise 2 applies it here.

### Testing one forecast against another

Two forecasts of the same series are compared on their squared errors. Write
$e^0_{t+1} = r^e_{t+1} - \bar{r}^e_t$ for the mean's error, $e^1_{t+1}$ for
the model's, and $d_{t+1} = (e^0_{t+1})^2 - (e^1_{t+1})^2$ for the loss
differential. @diebold1995 observed that under the null of equal accuracy $d$
has mean zero, so the test is a $t$-test on its mean with a standard error that
allows the losses to be serially correlated and heteroskedastic,

$$
\text{DM} = \frac{\bar{d}}{\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\bar{d})}},
$$ {#eq-16-dm}

with the variance estimated as in @eq-05-neweywest, asymptotically standard
normal. When the two models are nested, as a predictive regression and the
historical mean are, the larger model estimates parameters whose true value is
zero under the null and pays for them in forecast variance, so its squared
errors exceed the mean's even when the signal is useless and @eq-16-dm is
biased against it. @clark2007 correct this by adding back the term the
estimation noise contributes,

$$
\text{CW} = \frac{\overline{d_{t+1} + \left(\bar{r}^e_t - \hat{r}^e_{t+1}\right)^2}}
                 {\sqrt{\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\cdot)}},
$$ {#eq-16-cw}

read against the normal distribution as a one-sided test. It is the statistic
reported below whenever a signal is set against the mean, with @eq-16-dm
beside it to show what the correction changes.

### Why a small $R^2$ can matter

An $R^2_{\text{OS}}$ of half a percent looks like nothing, and it is not.
@kandel1996 showed that the decision of a mean-variance investor responds to a
predictive relation far weaker than any statistical test would accept, because
what the investor cares about is not the fit but the position the forecast
changes. The link is short. Under @eq-03-quadratic-utility an investor with
risk aversion $\gamma$ facing one risky asset with conditional mean $\mu_t$
and variance $\sigma^2$ holds $w_t = \mu_t / (\gamma\sigma^2)$ and earns an
expected excess return of $\mathbb{E}[\mu_t^2]/(\gamma\sigma^2)$. Using the
unconditional mean $\mu$ instead earns $\mu^2/(\gamma\sigma^2) = S^2/\gamma$,
with $S = \mu/\sigma$ the Sharpe ratio; the difference is
$\operatorname{Var}(\mu_t)/(\gamma\sigma^2)$, and
$\operatorname{Var}(\mu_t)/\sigma^2$ is the $R^2$ of the forecast. So, as
@campbell2008 write it,

$$
\Delta\,\mathbb{E}[r^e] \approx \frac{R^2_{\text{OS}}}{\gamma},
\qquad
\frac{\Delta\,\mathbb{E}[r^e]}{S^2/\gamma} \approx \frac{R^2_{\text{OS}}}{S^2}.
$$ {#eq-16-ct}

The proportional gain is the $R^2$ relative to the *squared* Sharpe ratio, and
monthly Sharpe ratios are small numbers. Take $R^2_{\text{OS}} = 0.5\%$ a
month, an annual Sharpe ratio of $0.5$ so that
$S = 0.5/\sqrt{12} = `r sprintf("%.3f", 0.5 / sqrt(12))`$ and
$S^2 = `r sprintf("%.4f", (0.5 / sqrt(12))^2)`$, and $\gamma = 5$: the
proportional gain is
$`r sprintf("%.3f", 0.005)` / `r sprintf("%.4f", (0.5 / sqrt(12))^2)`
= `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * 0.005 / (0.5 / sqrt(12))^2)`$ of the
unconditional expected excess return, and in return units
$0.005 / 5 = `r sprintf("%.0f", 1e4 * 0.005 / 5)`$ basis points a month,
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * 12 * 0.005 / 5)` percentage points a year. That is
what a predictive $R^2$ no referee would find impressive is worth to an
investor who acts on it without constraint, and it is why in-sample
significance and out-of-sample profit are different questions: the first asks
whether $\boldsymbol{b}$ is distinguishable from zero, the second whether
acting on $\hat{\boldsymbol{b}}$, estimated with error and passed through a
position rule and a cost model, beats not acting. @pesaran1995 made the same
point with switching rules run in real time.

The criterion that answers the second question is the certainty equivalent of
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory. For a strategy whose realized
excess returns have mean $\hat{\mu}_p$ and variance $\hat{\sigma}^2_p$ over
the out-of-sample months,

$$
\text{CE}_p = \hat{\mu}_p - \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\hat{\sigma}^2_p,
\qquad
\Delta = \text{CE}_{\text{forecast}} - \text{CE}_{\text{mean}},
$$ {#eq-16-cer}

is the riskless excess return the investor would accept in place of each, and
$\Delta$ is the fee she would pay to switch from the strategy built on the mean
to the one built on the forecast. It is computed from realized returns, gross
or net of costs, and it decides @sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-application.
What it does not do is score the forecast itself, independently of a position
rule. That measure, the risk-adjusted forecast error that
@sec-08-estimation-error-application introduced and
@sec-26-forecast-error-cost-theory derives, expresses a forecast's error as
the Sharpe ratio it costs [@salcher2026]; whether a forecaster should be
trained on that loss rather than on squared error is the question of
@sec-27-decision-aware-forecasting-theory.

### Which signals this universe can carry

The literature's signals fall into three families, and the shipped data
support two of them.

**Momentum** needs nothing but the return history. @jegadeesh1993 documented
that stocks which rose over the past three to twelve months continue to rise
over the next, and the construction that became standard skips the most recent
month to avoid short-term reversal: the signal at $t$ is the return over months
$t-11$ to $t-1$,

$$
\text{mom}_{i,t} = \prod_{k=1}^{11}\left(1 + R_{i,t-k}\right) - 1 .
$$ {#eq-16-mom}

@moskowitz2012 showed that the sign of an asset's own past twelve-month excess
return forecasts its next month across fifty-eight futures on equity indices,
bonds, currencies and commodities, the asset-class level of this book rather
than the stock level, and @asness2013 found value and momentum premia in every
class and region they examined, negatively correlated with each other.
**Value** is the family this universe cannot support: it needs a fundamental,
a book value or an earnings stream, that the market does not carry, so the
chapter builds momentum without its partner and the value side waits for
@sec-21-equity-sleeve-theory.

**Macro state** signals are the family @welch2008 tested: the dividend yield,
the term spread, the default spread, the short rate, inflation. @fama1989
showed that the term spread and the default spread forecast the excess returns
on stocks and bonds together, tracking business conditions, and both are in the
shipped data. `sim_curve_weekly`, described in
@sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market, carries the level, slope and
curvature of a @nelson1987 curve per region in the dynamic form of
@diebold2006, plus an investment-grade and a high-yield credit spread per
region. In that parametrization the slope factor is the short end minus the
long end, so the **term spread** of @fama1989 is minus the slope, and the
**IG spread** is their default spread. These are the same predictors, built
inside the universe: the bond block was simulated from them, so a signal that
forecasts the bond and credit series here is forecasting the state that
generated them, the state @sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-theory decomposes the
bond returns on. Whether it forecasts the equity series is the open question.

**Cross-sectional dispersion** is the third family, and it is the one
@sec-05-factor-models-application already built. The turbulence index of
@chow1999 and @kritzman2010, the Mahalanobis distance of a month's return
vector from its trailing mean in @eq-05-turbulence, measures how unusual the
pattern across the sixteen series is; @stoeckl2022turbulence show that
dispersion measured within a cross-section forecasts the premia earned on it,
and @stoeckl2022pu link the same construction to parameter uncertainty and to
the aggregate premium. It is a signal about the whole market rather than about
one series, so it enters every regression with the same value and a
series-specific slope.

The real-world versions of the macro signals are one call away for a reader
with a network connection: `tidyfinance` serves the @welch2008 predictor file,
whose `tms` and `dfy` columns are the term and default spreads built below;
the dates are any range of the predictor file's own, real calendar.

```{r}
#| label: goyal-welch
#| eval: false
gw <- tidyfinance::download_data_macro_predictors(
  dataset = "macro_predictors_monthly",
  start_date = "2000-01-01", end_date = "2020-12-31")   # an illustrative range
gw[, c("date", "tms", "dfy", "dp")]
```

Nothing below depends on it; every signal is built from the shipped data so
that the chapter reproduces offline.

## Building and Testing the Signals {#sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-implementation}

### Signals at month end, lagged once

Momentum first. @eq-16-mom is a ratio of two lagged values of the total-return
index, and the assertion checks it against the product it is meant to be.

```{r}
#| label: momentum
P   <- cumprod(1 + R)                                   # total-return index
mom <- xts::lag.xts(P, 1) / xts::lag.xts(P, 12) - 1     # months t-11 .. t-1; month t skipped
k <- 100L
stopifnot(all.equal(as.numeric(mom[k, ]),
                    unname(apply(1 + zoo::coredata(R)[(k - 11):(k - 1), ], 2, prod) - 1)))
```

The curve is weekly and the returns are monthly, so each month end takes the
last weekly observation on or before it, never after. The sign convention is
then checked against the data rather than assumed: the short rate in the
@diebold2006 parametrization is level plus slope, so level minus term spread
must track the bill.

```{r}
#| label: curve
cv <- sim_curve_weekly |>
  dplyr::filter(series %in% c("US_Level", "US_Slope", "US_IG_Spread", "US_HY_Spread")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = series, values_from = value) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date)
i_last <- findInterval(dates, cv$date)          # last weekly row on or before each month end
# Weekly dates are six to eight days apart, so the matched week is at most
# seven days before the month end and never after it.
stopifnot(all(cv$date[i_last] <= dates), all(dates - cv$date[i_last] < 8))

curve <- xts::xts(cbind(level = cv$US_Level[i_last],
                        term  = -cv$US_Slope[i_last],           # long minus short, in pp
                        ig    = 100 * cv$US_IG_Spread[i_last],  # pp
                        hy    = 100 * cv$US_HY_Spread[i_last]),
                  order.by = dates)

cor_short <- stats::cor(as.numeric(curve$level - curve$term),
                        100 * sim_riskfree_monthly$rate_annual)
stopifnot(cor_short > 0.9)
round(cor_short, 3)
```

The correlation between the curve's implied short rate and the bill is
`r sprintf("%.3f", cor_short)`, and the assertion would have failed the render
at a sign error. The turbulence index is @sec-05-factor-models-application's
call, unchanged: a sixty-month trailing window, so the index for month $t$ is
computed from the moments of months $t-60$ to $t-1$ and the return vector of
$t$ itself.

```{r}
#| label: turbulence
turb <- uncertaintymeasures::OSturbulence(R, rolling = TRUE, roll.obs = 60)$turb
colnames(turb) <- "turb"
common <- merge(curve, turb)
stopifnot(identical(zoo::index(common), dates))
```

Every signal now sits at the month end it was observed. Shifting the whole
block forward by one month puts the signal observed at $t$ on the row of the
return it predicts, $t+1$, and the assertion states that the shift did what it
was meant to do.

```{r}
#| label: lag
common_lag <- xts::lag.xts(common, 1)
mom_lag    <- xts::lag.xts(mom, 1)
rev_lag    <- xts::lag.xts(Re, 1)                       # last month's own excess return
stopifnot(all.equal(as.numeric(common_lag[k + 1, ]), as.numeric(common[k, ])),
          all.equal(as.numeric(mom_lag[k + 1, ]),    as.numeric(mom[k, ])),
          is.na(common_lag[1, "term"]))

# For one series: the excess return in month m beside every signal as it stood
# at the end of m - 1. This is the frame @eq-16-predictive is estimated on.
pairs_of <- function(s) {
  data.frame(date = dates, y = as.numeric(Re[, s]),
             mom = as.numeric(mom_lag[, s]), rev = as.numeric(rev_lag[, s]),
             zoo::coredata(common_lag))
}
first_row <- function(v) min(which(!is.na(pairs_of("US_equity")[[v]])))
c(momentum = first_row("mom"), curve = first_row("term"), turbulence = first_row("turb"))
```

The first row carries no signal, the momentum column begins in month
`r first_row("mom")` and turbulence, which needs sixty months of history, in
month `r first_row("turb")`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-16-signals
#| fig-cap: "The four signals as they stood at each month end. The term spread and the IG spread are read off the US curve in percentage points; turbulence is the sixty-month out-of-sample Mahalanobis distance of chapter 5; momentum is the 12-1 return of `US_equity`, one of sixteen such series."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.55
sig_pts <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(date = dates, value = as.numeric(common$term), signal = "term spread (pp)"),
  tibble::tibble(date = dates, value = as.numeric(common$ig),   signal = "IG spread (pp)"),
  tibble::tibble(date = dates, value = as.numeric(common$turb), signal = "turbulence"),
  tibble::tibble(date = dates, value = as.numeric(mom[, "US_equity"]),
                 signal = "12-1 momentum, US_equity")
) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(signal = factor(signal, levels = c("term spread (pp)", "IG spread (pp)",
                                                   "turbulence", "12-1 momentum, US_equity")))

ggplot2::ggplot(sig_pts, ggplot2::aes(date, value)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.25, colour = tidyaa_colors[["rule"]]) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = tidyaa_colors[["blue"]], linewidth = 0.45) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~ signal, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_model() +
  ggplot2::labs(y = NULL)
```

### In sample: sixty-four regressions

Each series is regressed on each of the four signals over the whole sample, one
signal at a time, with the standard errors of @eq-05-neweywest at six lags as
in @sec-05-factor-models-implementation.

```{r}
#| label: insample
sig4 <- c(mom = "12-1 momentum", term = "term spread", ig = "IG spread", turb = "turbulence")

nw_t <- function(m, j = 2L) {
  nw <- sandwich::NeweyWest(m, lag = 6, prewhite = FALSE)
  unname(stats::coef(m)[j] / sqrt(nw[j, j]))
}

ins <- lapply(colnames(Re), function(s) {
  d <- pairs_of(s)
  lapply(names(sig4), function(v) {
    dd <- d[!is.na(d[[v]]), ]
    m  <- stats::lm(y ~ x, data = data.frame(y = dd$y, x = dd[[v]]))
    tibble::tibble(series = s, signal = v, slope = unname(stats::coef(m)[2]),
                   t = nw_t(m), r2 = summary(m)$r.squared, n = nrow(dd))
  }) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()

ins_sum <- ins |>
  dplyr::group_by(signal) |>
  dplyr::summarise(positive = sum(slope > 0), t_above_2 = sum(abs(t) > 2),
                   t_above_3 = sum(abs(t) > 3), median_r2 = median(r2), max_r2 = max(r2))
ins_sum
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-16-insample
#| tbl-cap: "In-sample predictive regressions of each series' monthly excess return on each signal, one at a time, over the full sample. Cells are the Newey-West t-statistic of the slope with the R² of @eq-16-r2 in brackets."
#| echo: false
ins |>
  dplyr::mutate(cell = sprintf("%+.2f (%.1f%%)", t, 100 * r2),
                signal = factor(signal, levels = names(sig4))) |>
  dplyr::select(series, signal, cell) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = signal, values_from = cell) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrr", col.names = c("", unname(sig4)))
```

```{r}
#| label: insample-facts
#| include: false
at_ins <- function(v, col) ins_sum[[col]][ins_sum$signal == v]
t_of   <- function(s, v) ins$t[ins$series == s & ins$signal == v]
best_term <- ins |> dplyr::filter(signal == "term") |> dplyr::slice_max(abs(t), n = 1)
n_bond <- sum(grepl("_government$|_credit$", colnames(Re)))
term_bond_pos <- sum(ins$slope[ins$signal == "term" & grepl("_government$|_credit$", ins$series)] > 0)
mom_eq_neg <- sum(ins$slope[ins$signal == "mom" & grepl("_equity$", ins$series)] < 0)
n_above <- sort(ins_sum$t_above_2, decreasing = TRUE)
stopifnot(term_bond_pos == n_bond,
          at_ins("term", "t_above_2") == n_above[1],      # the strongest column
          at_ins("ig", "t_above_2") == n_above[2],        # the second
          at_ins("mom", "t_above_2") == 0L,               # momentum clears two nowhere
          all(ins$slope[ins$signal == "mom" & grepl("_government$", ins$series)] > 0))
```

Read @tbl-16-insample by column. The term spread is the strongest signal in
the table: its slope is positive for `r at_ins("term", "positive")` of the
sixteen series, among them every one of the `r n_bond` bond and credit
series, `r at_ins("term", "t_above_2")` of its $t$-statistics exceed two and
`r {n3 <- at_ins("term", "t_above_3"); if (n3 == 0L) "none exceeds three" else if (n3 == 1L) "one exceeds three" else paste(n3, "exceed three")}`,
the largest being `r best_term$series` at `r sprintf("%.2f", best_term$t)`.
That is @fama1989 on
modeled data: a steep curve forecasts high excess returns on bonds. The IG
spread is second, with `r at_ins("ig", "t_above_2")` above two, again on the
credit and bond series where the state was built in. Turbulence clears two on
`r at_ins("turb", "t_above_2")` series and its median $R^2$ is
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * at_ins("turb", "median_r2"))`. Momentum clears two
nowhere: its slope is negative for
`r if (mom_eq_neg == 5L) "all five" else paste(mom_eq_neg, "of the five")`
equity series, positive for the government series, and its largest $R^2$ is
`r sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * at_ins("mom", "max_r2"))`. The premium
@moskowitz2012 document in futures is not in these class indices at a monthly
horizon; they found it across fifty-eight instruments with a sign rule, not one
series at a time with a slope. The largest $R^2$ anywhere in the table is
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * max(ins$r2))`, which by @eq-16-ct is not a small
number. The question is whether any of it is available in real time.

### Out of sample: an expanding window from model year 11

The out-of-sample scheme is an expanding window with a burn-in, and
`rsample::rolling_origin()` describes the same sequence of splits in the
vocabulary of `tidymodels`, so the count of splits is asserted to match.

```{r}
#| label: oos-setup
burn <- 120L
oos  <- seq.int(burn + 1L, nrow(Re))       # forecast months 121 .. 372
stopifnot(model_year(dates[oos[1]]) == 11L)   # the register's out-of-sample start

ols_fc <- function(d, v, m) {
  tr <- which(!is.na(d[[v]]) & seq_len(nrow(d)) < m)          # strictly before m
  b  <- stats::lm.fit(cbind(1, d[[v]][tr]), d$y[tr])$coefficients
  unname(b[1] + b[2] * d[[v]][m])
}

splits <- rsample::rolling_origin(data.frame(m = seq_len(nrow(Re))),
                                  initial = burn, assess = 1, cumulative = TRUE)
stopifnot(nrow(splits) == length(oos))
c(forecast_months = length(oos), first = fmt_model(dates[oos[1]]))
```

The burn-in is the first `r burn` months; forecasts begin in
`r fmt_model(dates[oos[1]])` and run to the end of the sample,
`r length(oos)` months, which are the months the register of
@sec-25-backtesting-application scores. At each month $m$ in that range the
regression is fit on every pair dated before $m$ where the signal exists, the
forecast is made for $m$, and the historical mean of the excess return through
$m-1$ is recorded beside it.

One signal at a time is what @welch2008 tested and what a practitioner rarely
does. With seven predictors per series, the four above plus last month's
return, the high-yield spread and the level of the curve, least squares on
sixty to three hundred months fits noise, and the remedy is to shrink. The
elastic net of @zou2005 minimizes the squared error plus a penalty
$\lambda\left[\alpha\|\boldsymbol{b}\|_1 + (1-\alpha)\|\boldsymbol{b}\|_2^2/2\right]$,
which at $\alpha = 1/2$ both shrinks coefficients toward zero and sets some
exactly to zero; @gu2020 use it as the first of their machine-learning
forecasters for the cross-section of stock returns, and @coqueret2020 give the
algorithm and its `glmnet` implementation, which we do not reproduce. What
matters here is the tuning, because it is where the future leaks in: $\lambda$
is chosen by five-fold cross-validation on contiguous blocks of the training
window, in time order rather than shuffled, re-tuned once a year, and the
coefficients are refit every month on the data through $m-1$. Two values of
$\lambda$ are kept, the one that minimizes cross-validated error and the most
penalized one within a standard error of it, because the choice turns out to
matter.

```{r}
#| label: enet
en_vars <- c("mom", "rev", "term", "ig", "hy", "level", "turb")

enet_fc <- function(d) {
  ok  <- stats::complete.cases(d[, en_vars])
  lam <- c(NA_real_, NA_real_)
  t(vapply(oos, function(m) {
    tr <- which(ok & seq_len(nrow(d)) < m)
    X  <- as.matrix(d[tr, en_vars]); y <- d$y[tr]
    if ((m - oos[1]) %% 12L == 0L) {                      # re-tune once a year
      fold <- ceiling(seq_along(tr) / (length(tr) / 5))   # five contiguous blocks
      cvf  <- glmnet::cv.glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0.5, foldid = fold)
      lam <<- c(cvf$lambda.min, cvf$lambda.1se)
    }
    fit <- glmnet::glmnet(X, y, alpha = 0.5)
    as.numeric(stats::predict(fit, newx = as.matrix(d[m, en_vars]), s = lam))
  }, numeric(2)))
}
```

The loop below produces, for every series and every out-of-sample month, the
historical mean, the four single-signal forecasts, their equal-weighted
combination, which @rapach2010 showed is more stable than any of its parts,
and the two elastic-net forecasts.

```{r}
#| label: forecasts
fc <- lapply(colnames(Re), function(s) {
  d <- pairs_of(s)
  out <- data.frame(date = dates[oos], series = s, y = d$y[oos],
                    mean = vapply(oos, function(m) mean(d$y[seq_len(m - 1L)]), numeric(1)))
  for (v in names(sig4)) out[[v]] <- vapply(oos, function(m) ols_fc(d, v, m), numeric(1))
  out$comb <- rowMeans(out[, names(sig4)])
  en <- enet_fc(d); out$enet_min <- en[, 1]; out$enet_1se <- en[, 2]
  out
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
stopifnot(nrow(fc) == N * length(oos), !anyNA(fc))
```

@eq-16-r2os, @eq-16-cw and @eq-16-dm are then three short functions.

```{r}
#| label: oos-stats
models <- c(names(sig4), "comb", "enet_min", "enet_1se")
model_label <- c(sig4, comb = "combination",
                 enet_min = "elastic net, lambda.min", enet_1se = "elastic net, lambda.1se")

r2_os <- function(y, f, f0) 1 - sum((y - f)^2) / sum((y - f0)^2)
cw_t  <- function(y, f, f0) nw_t(stats::lm(I((y - f0)^2 - (y - f)^2 + (f0 - f)^2) ~ 1), 1L)
dm_t  <- function(y, f, f0) nw_t(stats::lm(I((y - f0)^2 - (y - f)^2) ~ 1), 1L)

oos_tbl <- fc |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(dplyr::all_of(models), names_to = "model", values_to = "f") |>
  dplyr::group_by(series, model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(r2os = r2_os(y, f, mean), cw = cw_t(y, f, mean), dm = dm_t(y, f, mean),
                   .groups = "drop") |>
  dplyr::mutate(model = factor(model, levels = models))

oos_sum <- oos_tbl |>
  dplyr::group_by(model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(positive = sum(r2os > 0), median_r2os = median(r2os), best = max(r2os),
                   cw_above = sum(cw > 1.645), dm_above = sum(dm > 1.645))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-16-oos-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Out-of-sample R² of @eq-16-r2os against the expanding historical mean, summarized across the sixteen series over every forecast month after the burn-in. The last two columns count the series on which the forecast beats the mean at the one-sided five percent level, by the Clark-West statistic of @eq-16-cw and by the uncorrected Diebold-Mariano statistic of @eq-16-dm."
#| echo: false
oos_sum |>
  dplyr::transmute(model = unname(model_label[as.character(model)]),
                   positive = sprintf("%d of %d", positive, N),
                   median_r2os = sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * median_r2os),
                   best = sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * best),
                   cw_above = cw_above, dm_above = dm_above) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "R²OS > 0", "median R²OS", "best R²OS", "CW > 1.645", "DM > 1.645"))
```

```{r}
#| label: oos-facts
#| include: false
at_oos <- function(mdl, col) oos_sum[[col]][oos_sum$model == mdl]
term_best <- oos_tbl |> dplyr::filter(model == "term") |> dplyr::slice_max(r2os, n = 1)
turb_worst <- oos_tbl |> dplyr::filter(model == "turb") |> dplyr::slice_min(r2os, n = 1)
single_med <- oos_sum$median_r2os[oos_sum$model %in% names(sig4)]
stopifnot(at_oos("term", "positive") == max(oos_sum$positive),          # the term spread survives
          at_oos("term", "positive") > at_oos("enet_1se", "positive"),   # the net stays short of it
          at_oos("enet_1se", "positive") > at_oos("enet_min", "positive"),
          at_oos("enet_1se", "median_r2os") > at_oos("enet_min", "median_r2os"),
          dplyr::between(at_oos("comb", "median_r2os"), min(single_med), max(single_med)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-16-oos
#| fig-cap: "Out-of-sample R² by series and forecast, from one data frame. Series are ordered by the term spread's value. Anything left of the vertical line lost to the historical mean over the same months."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.7
ord <- oos_tbl |> dplyr::filter(model == "term") |> dplyr::arrange(r2os) |> dplyr::pull(series)
oos_tbl |>
  dplyr::mutate(series = factor(series, levels = ord),
                model = factor(unname(model_label[as.character(model)]),
                               levels = unname(model_label))) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(100 * r2os, series, colour = model)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = tidyaa_colors[["ink"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.2, alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_tidyaa() +
  ggplot2::guides(colour = ggplot2::guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "out-of-sample R², percent", y = NULL)
```

Three findings, in decreasing order of comfort.

The term spread survives. Its $R^2_{\text{OS}}$ is positive on
`r at_oos("term", "positive")` of the sixteen series, its median is
`r sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * at_oos("term", "median_r2os"))`, and it beats the
mean by the Clark-West test on `r at_oos("term", "cw_above")` of them, with
`r term_best$series` at `r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * term_best$r2os)`. The
uncorrected statistic of @eq-16-dm finds `r at_oos("term", "dm_above")`, which
is the nesting bias of @clark2007 in one column: the regression carries two
estimated parameters whose noise the mean does not pay for, and without the
correction that noise is scored against the signal. The IG spread, second in
sample, keeps a positive $R^2_{\text{OS}}$ on `r at_oos("ig", "positive")`
series and turbulence on `r at_oos("turb", "positive")`; the in-sample fit of
the first was concentrated in credit and of the second in a few crisis months,
and an expanding window estimated before those months cannot see either.
Turbulence's worst case is `r turb_worst$series` at
`r sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * turb_worst$r2os)`.

The combination helps and does not rescue. Averaging the four forecasts, the
rule of @rapach2010, is positive on `r at_oos("comb", "positive")` series with
a median of `r sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * at_oos("comb", "median_r2os"))`,
between its best and its worst constituent, which is what an average does.

The elastic net loses. At the cross-validated minimum it beats the mean on
`r at_oos("enet_min", "positive")` series with a median $R^2_{\text{OS}}$ of
`r sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * at_oos("enet_min", "median_r2os"))`; at the more
penalized `lambda.1se` the median rises to
`r sprintf("%+.2f%%", 100 * at_oos("enet_1se", "median_r2os"))` and the count
to `r at_oos("enet_1se", "positive")`, still short of the single term spread.
This is what @gu2020 report for the same model on the cross-section of stocks,
where the elastic net is the weakest of their forecasters and its gains come
from thousands of stocks and hundreds of signals, not from seven signals on
sixteen series. The more the model is allowed to fit, the more it fits the
burn-in's noise, and the rule that shrinks hardest is the one that comes
closest to the mean it is trying to beat. The lesson of
@sec-08-estimation-error-theory, that the cost of an input is set by how well
it can be estimated, applies to a conditional mean as it applied to an
unconditional one.

## The Economic Value of a Tilt {#sec-16-signals-and-forecasts-application}

### A tilt around the policy

The strategic policy is the equal-weight portfolio of @eq-08-ew, built through
the package's own `equal.weight()` as in
@sec-08-estimation-error-implementation. It is the anchor because it estimates
nothing, so that every difference between it and the tilted portfolio is
attributable to the forecast, and because the constrained minimum-variance
portfolio of @sec-09-mean-variance-implementation holds most of its weight in
one series and leaves no room to tilt.

```{r}
#| label: policy
base_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")
w_policy <- extractWeights(equal.weight(Re, base_spec))[colnames(Re)]
stopifnot(all.equal(unname(w_policy), rep(1 / N, N)))
```

The tilt converts a forecast into a weight in three steps. The forecast for
month $t+1$ is divided by the series' trailing sixty-month volatility, both
known at $t$, so that a forecast of one percent means something different on a
government bond than on an equity market; the cross-sectional mean is removed,
because under full investment only a relative view can be expressed; and the
result is scaled by $\kappa$ and clipped to a band of $\pm\delta$ around the
policy weight,

$$
s_{i,t} = \frac{\hat{r}^e_{i,t+1}}{\hat{\sigma}_{i,t}}
        - \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\hat{r}^e_{j,t+1}}{\hat{\sigma}_{j,t}},
\qquad
w_{i,t} = w^{\text{policy}}_i + \operatorname{clip}\!\left(\kappa\,s_{i,t},\,-\delta,\,\delta\right),
$$ {#eq-16-tilt}

re-centered so that the weights sum to one. With $\delta = 1/(2N)$ no weight
can fall below zero or above three halves of the policy weight, and $\kappa$
is set so that a forecast Sharpe ratio of one half a year fills the band. The
weights for month $t+1$ are set at the end of month $t$ from forecasts made at
$t$, which is the dating @eq-16-predictive was built on.

```{r}
#| label: tilt
vol60 <- zoo::rollapply(Re, 60, stats::sd, align = "right", fill = NA)
band  <- 0.5 / N
kappa <- band / (0.5 / sqrt(12))              # a forecast Sharpe ratio of 0.5 a year fills the band

tilt_weights <- function(model) {
  F <- fc |> dplyr::select(date, series, f = dplyr::all_of(model)) |>
    tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = series, values_from = f)
  Fm <- as.matrix(F[, colnames(Re)])
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(Fm), colnames(Re)), nrow(Fm) == length(oos))
  W <- t(vapply(seq_len(nrow(Fm)), function(i) {
    m  <- oos[i]
    s  <- Fm[i, ] / as.numeric(vol60[m - 1L, ])       # forecast in volatility units, known at m - 1
    s  <- s - mean(s)                                  # relative view
    tl <- pmin(pmax(kappa * s, -band), band)
    w  <- w_policy + tl - mean(tl)
    w  <- pmax(w, 0); w / sum(w)
  }, numeric(N)))
  dimnames(W) <- list(as.character(dates[oos]), colnames(Re))
  stopifnot(all(abs(rowSums(W) - 1) < 1e-12), all(W >= 0))
  W
}

W_policy <- matrix(1 / N, length(oos), N, dimnames = list(as.character(dates[oos]), colnames(Re)))
W_term   <- tilt_weights("term")
c(mean_abs_tilt = mean(abs(W_term - 1 / N)),
  share_at_band = mean(abs(abs(W_term - 1 / N) - band) < 1e-9))
```

The term-spread tilt moves the average weight by
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(abs(W_term - 1 / N)))` percentage points
against a band of `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * band)`, and the band binds on
`r {sh <- mean(abs(abs(W_term - 1 / N) - band) < 1e-9); if (sh == 0) "none" else sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * sh)}`
of the weights. The forecasts are modest and so is the tilt.

::: {.callout-note}
## `applyFUN()` and `trailingFUN()` do not roll anything

The two exported utilities whose names suggest they were written for this
chapter were not. `applyFUN(R, weights, FUN)` evaluates one risk or return
function, by name, for a weight vector or for every row of a weight matrix on
the *whole* of `R`; it is the helper behind `chart.Scatter()`, which uses it
to place random portfolios on the risk-return plane. `trailingFUN(R, weights,
n, FUN, FUNargs)` evaluates `FUN` once on the last `n + 1` rows of `R`, not
the last `n`, and returns one number. Neither produces a time series. Rolling
estimation in this book is `zoo::rollapply()`, as in
@sec-05-factor-models-application and the `vol60` line above, or the explicit
loop of `enet_fc()`. Both are run here so that the behavior is measured
rather than described.
:::

```{r}
#| label: applyfun
# applyFUN: one metric, many static weight vectors, the full return history.
applyFUN(Re, weights = rbind(policy = w_policy, average_tilt = colMeans(W_term)),
         FUN = "StdDev")

# trailingFUN: FUN once, on the last n + 1 rows. n = 11 gives twelve months.
x  <- Re[, "US_equity"]
tf <- trailingFUN(x, weights = NULL, n = 11, FUN = "mean", FUNargs = list())
stopifnot(all.equal(tf, mean(utils::tail(as.numeric(x), 12))))
c(trailingFUN_n11 = tf,
  mean_last_12 = mean(utils::tail(as.numeric(x), 12)),
  mean_last_11 = mean(utils::tail(as.numeric(x), 11)))
```

### Rebalancing, turnover and costs

The portfolio is rebalanced monthly. Its accounting is written out rather than
handed to `Return.portfolio()`, because that function back-fills equal weights
before the first supplied weight vector, the trap
@sec-23-rebalancing-implementation documents, and because the drifted weights
are needed for the cost. By the end of month $t+1$ each weight has drifted to
$w^{-}_{i,t+1} = w_{i,t}(1 + R_{i,t+1}) / (1 + r_{p,t+1})$; the trade back to
the target has the turnover of @eq-23-turnover and costs what @eq-23-net
charges, at the per-class one-way rates of `pm_costs_default()` that
@sec-23-rebalancing-application uses on the register, mapped to each series by
its class suffix.

```{r}
#| label: accounting
cost_rate <- pm_costs_default()[sub(".*_", "", colnames(Re))]
stopifnot(!anyNA(cost_rate)); names(cost_rate) <- colnames(Re)

run_path <- function(W) {
  Rm <- zoo::coredata(R)[oos, colnames(Re), drop = FALSE]
  stopifnot(identical(colnames(W), colnames(Re)), nrow(W) == nrow(Rm))
  r       <- rowSums(W * Rm)                                  # month t+1, weights set at t
  drifted <- W * (1 + Rm) / (1 + r)                            # weights before the trade
  trade   <- abs(W[-1, , drop = FALSE] - drifted[-nrow(W), , drop = FALSE])
  tibble::tibble(date = dates[oos], gross = r,
                 turnover = c(rowSums(trade) / 2, 0),
                 cost     = c(as.numeric(trade %*% cost_rate), 0)) |>
    dplyr::mutate(net = gross - cost)
}

# Sharpe ratio as the register computes it: compounded, in excess of the bill.
sharpe_realized <- function(r, rf) {
  n <- length(r)
  (prod(1 + r)^(12 / n) - prod(1 + rf)^(12 / n)) / (stats::sd(r) * sqrt(12))
}
gamma <- 5
summarise_path <- function(p, label) {
  rf_o <- rf[oos]
  ce <- function(r) { e <- r - rf_o; 12 * mean(e) - gamma / 2 * 12 * stats::var(e) }
  tibble::tibble(
    portfolio    = label,
    ret          = prod(1 + p$gross)^(12 / nrow(p)) - 1,
    vol          = stats::sd(p$gross) * sqrt(12),
    sharpe_gross = sharpe_realized(p$gross, rf_o),
    turnover     = 12 * mean(p$turnover),
    cost_drag    = 12 * mean(p$cost),
    sharpe_net   = sharpe_realized(p$net, rf_o),
    max_dd       = as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::maxDrawdown(xts::xts(p$net, order.by = p$date))),
    ce_net       = ce(p$net))
}

tilts <- c(mom = "momentum", term = "term spread", comb = "combination",
           enet_min = "elastic net, lambda.min", enet_1se = "elastic net, lambda.1se")
paths <- c(list(policy = run_path(W_policy)),
           lapply(names(tilts), function(k) run_path(tilt_weights(k))) |> setNames(names(tilts)))
res <- dplyr::bind_rows(Map(summarise_path, paths, c("equal weight (policy)", unname(tilts)))) |>
  dplyr::mutate(ce_gain = ce_net - ce_net[1])
```

```{r}
#| label: tilt-facts
#| include: false
g <- function(k, col) res[[col]][res$portfolio == c(policy = "equal weight (policy)", tilts)[[k]]]
se_sr <- sqrt((1 + (g("policy", "sharpe_net") / sqrt(12))^2 / 2) / length(oos)) * sqrt(12)
paid  <- names(tilts)[vapply(names(tilts), function(k) g(k, "ce_gain") > 0, logical(1))]
stopifnot(g("term", "ce_gain") == max(res$ce_gain),           # the term spread pays most
          sum(res$ce_gain > 10e-4) == 1L,                      # and alone by more than ten basis points
          g("term", "max_dd") < g("policy", "max_dd"),
          g("mom", "ce_gain") < 0, g("enet_min", "ce_gain") < 0,
          g("term", "sharpe_net") - g("policy", "sharpe_net") < se_sr)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-16-relative
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative log return of each tilt relative to the policy, net of costs, from one data frame. A rising line is a tilt that is ahead of equal weighting at that date."
#| echo: false
#| fig-asp: 0.55
rel <- lapply(names(tilts), function(k) {
  tibble::tibble(date = paths[[k]]$date, kind = tilts[[k]],
                 value = cumsum(log1p(paths[[k]]$net)) - cumsum(log1p(paths$policy$net)))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows() |>
  dplyr::mutate(kind = factor(kind, levels = unname(tilts)))

ggplot2::ggplot(rel, ggplot2::aes(date, value, colour = kind)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = tidyaa_colors[["ink"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_tidyaa() +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_x_model() +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "cumulative log return relative to the policy, net")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-16-tilt
#| tbl-cap: "The equal-weight policy and five tilts on it, rebalanced monthly over the out-of-sample months. Returns annualized; the Sharpe ratio is compounded and in excess of the bill; turnover is annual; the cost drag is annual return lost to trading at the per-class rates of chapter 23; the drawdown and the certainty-equivalent gain of @eq-16-cer at gamma = 5 are net of costs."
#| echo: false
res |>
  dplyr::transmute(portfolio,
                   ret = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * ret), vol = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * vol),
                   sharpe_gross = sprintf("%.3f", sharpe_gross),
                   turnover = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * turnover),
                   cost_drag = sprintf("%.0f bp", 1e4 * cost_drag),
                   sharpe_net = sprintf("%.3f", sharpe_net),
                   max_dd = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * max_dd),
                   ce_gain = sprintf("%+.0f bp", 1e4 * ce_gain)) |>
  kable(align = "lrrrrrrrr",
        col.names = c("", "return", "volatility", "Sharpe, gross", "turnover", "cost drag",
                      "Sharpe, net", "max drawdown", "CE gain, net"))
```

### Reading the result

Of the five forecasts, `r length(paid)` leave the investor better off after
costs, and only one of them by more than a few basis points: the term spread,
the one signal that survived @tbl-16-oos-summary. Its tilt earns a net Sharpe
ratio of `r sprintf("%.3f", g("term", "sharpe_net"))` against the policy's
`r sprintf("%.3f", g("policy", "sharpe_net"))`, a certainty-equivalent gain of
`r sprintf("%.0f", 1e4 * g("term", "ce_gain"))` basis points a year at
$\gamma = 5$, with a slightly shallower drawdown and turnover of
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * g("term", "turnover"))` against
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * g("policy", "turnover"))`, which the per-class
rates price at `r sprintf("%.0f", 1e4 * g("term", "cost_drag"))` basis points
a year. The combination is a wash at
`r sprintf("%+.0f", 1e4 * g("comb", "ce_gain"))` basis points. Momentum loses
`r sprintf("%.0f", -1e4 * g("mom", "ce_gain"))` basis points, and the
least-penalized elastic net turns the portfolio over
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * g("enet_min", "turnover"))` a year, almost
`r sprintf("%.0f", g("enet_min", "turnover") / g("policy", "turnover"))`
times the policy's, to lose
`r sprintf("%.0f", -1e4 * g("enet_min", "ce_gain"))` net. A model that fits
noise trades on it, and @sec-23-rebalancing-application shows the same
monotone relation between how much a strategy estimates and how much it pays
to trade.

The gain that exists is small against its own uncertainty. The standard error
of an annualized Sharpe ratio estimated over `r length(oos)` months is, by
the formula of @lo2002 under independence, about `r sprintf("%.2f", se_sr)`;
the term tilt's advantage of
`r sprintf("%.3f", g("term", "sharpe_net") - g("policy", "sharpe_net"))` is
well inside it, and the paired test of @sec-25-backtesting-application, which
exploits the correlation of the two series, would be sharper but not by enough
to turn this into evidence. The honest reading is the one @campbell2008 gave
for the equity premium: the signal that theory motivates, the term structure
that @fama1989 tied to business conditions, is worth a little to an investor
who uses it with restraint, and the signals that data alone motivate are worth
nothing after costs. @sharpe1987 described tactical allocation as the
strategic policy re-solved with current information; on this universe the
re-solving is worth a few tens of basis points where the information is real
and costs about as much where it is not.

Two things this chapter did not do are done elsewhere. It built the forecasts
from data; a view that comes from an opinion and must become a return vector
before an optimizer can use it is the subject of
@sec-17-expressing-views-theory. And it scaled each forecast into a weight by
a rule chosen by hand, @eq-16-tilt; @sec-18-parametric-policies-theory skips
the forecast and estimates the map from signal to weight on the investor's
objective directly, in the manner of @brandt2009, while
@sec-19-regimes-theory lets the whole policy switch with a detected state
rather than tilt with a continuous signal. Whether any of the three should be
judged on squared forecast error at all is the question
@sec-26-forecast-error-cost-theory takes up.

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- A predictive regression is judged out of sample, against the historical
  mean, by the $R^2_{\text{OS}}$ of @eq-16-r2os, and against that nested
  benchmark by the Clark-West correction of @eq-16-cw to the Diebold-Mariano
  test, because the mean does not pay the estimation noise a regression does
  [@welch2008; @campbell2008; @diebold1995; @clark2007].
- A small $R^2$ is not a small effect. By @eq-16-ct the proportional gain to a
  mean-variance investor is $R^2_{\text{OS}} / S^2$, so half a percent a month
  against an annual Sharpe ratio of one half is a quarter of the expected
  excess return [@kandel1996].
- This universe supports momentum from returns, the term and credit spreads
  from `sim_curve_weekly`, and turbulence from the cross-section; it does not
  support value, which needs fundamentals it does not carry.
- Of four signals on sixteen series, the term spread is the only one with
  out-of-sample evidence, positive on `r at_oos("term", "positive")` series and
  significant on `r at_oos("term", "cw_above")`; momentum, the IG spread and
  turbulence lose to the mean out of sample, and a regularized seven-signal
  model loses on `r N - at_oos("enet_1se", "positive")` to
  `r N - at_oos("enet_min", "positive")` of the sixteen, the more of them the
  less it shrinks [@gu2020].
- A tilt of at most half the policy weight pays after costs on the term
  spread, by `r sprintf("%.0f", 1e4 * g("term", "ce_gain"))` basis points a
  year of certainty equivalent, inside the sampling error of the Sharpe ratio;
  the combination earns a few basis points, and momentum and the elastic net
  trade more and lose.
- `applyFUN()` scores static weight vectors on the full history and
  `trailingFUN()` evaluates a function once on the last `n + 1` rows. Neither
  rolls; rolling estimation is `zoo::rollapply()` or an explicit loop.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. The curve signals above are the US term spread and the US IG spread for
   every series. Replace them, for each non-US series, with the term spread
   and IG spread of the series' own region, keeping the US ones for
   `GLOBAL_commodity`, and recompute the term-spread points of @fig-16-oos.
   Does a local curve forecast a local bond better than the US curve does?
2. @campbell2008 set a forecast of the equity premium to zero whenever the
   regression produces a negative one. Apply the restriction to the
   term-spread forecasts of the five equity series and recompute their
   $R^2_{\text{OS}}$ and Clark-West statistics. Which series does the
   restriction help, and what does the answer say about the sign of the
   estimated slope in those months?
3. The tilt of @eq-16-tilt fills its band at a forecast Sharpe ratio of one
   half a year. Double $\kappa$ and halve it, and recompute @tbl-16-tilt for
   the term-spread and momentum tilts. Does the certainty-equivalent gain
   scale with $\kappa$, and which tilt is hurt more by a larger $\kappa$?
4. The tilt expresses only a relative view. For `US_equity` alone, implement
   the timing rule of @campbell2008, $w_t = \hat{r}^e_{t+1} / (\gamma\hat{\sigma}^2_t)$
   with the balance in the bill and the weight confined to $[0, 1.5]$, using
   the term-spread forecast and $\gamma = 5$, and compare its certainty
   equivalent with a constant weight of one. Does the absolute view earn what
   @eq-16-ct predicts from the series' $R^2_{\text{OS}}$?
